title: In Texas's Rio Grande Valley, the Deportation Drive Is Galvanising the Midterm Vote
excerpt: The Valley swung to Trump in 2024 over the border. Two years of domestic enforcement — a $180.6 million hit to the local economy, an ACLU poll showing 63 percent say ICE has gone too far, and deportations like a Progreso woman's within 36 hours of a hearing — are swinging it back days before the November 3 midterms.
body:
• In the Rio Grande Valley — which swung sharply to Donald Trump in 2024 — voters and organisers say the deportation drive, not border crossings, is now the defining issue days before the November 3 midterms.
  • An ACLU of Texas poll of 1,031 border residents found only 34 percent think state and local immigration enforcement makes their communities safer, while 53 percent say it makes life harder without improving safety and 63 percent say ICE tactics have gone too far.
  • The region has lost an estimated $180.6 million in economic activity under the administration's immigration policies, according to a Caminos Institute report cited in local reporting.
  • For Indian and other immigrant families in Texas: enforcement is now domestic, not just at the border — a missed court date led to one Progreso woman's deportation within 36 hours of a DHS hearing, a pattern immigration lawyers in the Valley say is repeating.

In Brownsville, in Texas's Rio Grande Valley, community organisers gathered over tamales, pan dulce and sugar skulls for a Dia de los Muertos vigil honouring victims of state violence, including people killed in immigration enforcement and detention. The vigil came just days before the US midterm election on November 3, in a region that helped propel Donald Trump in 2024 — and where his deportation policies may now bury Republicans, Al Jazeera reported from the Valley.

Mark Anthony Vasquez, a 52-year-old community organiser, described an atmosphere around ICE detentions and raids in which residents feel there is no real due process. Down the block, at a bookstore panel on border policy, 24-year-old Juliana Garcia was asking for advice on finding a lawyer who can navigate the administration's shifting rules.

Garcia's aunt, a well-known community member in the nearby border town of Progreso, was deported just weeks earlier. Called to a Department of Homeland Security hearing, she learned she had missed a court date tied to her immigration status and, in the stress of the moment, signed a voluntary deportation form. "Within 36 hours, she was deported," Garcia said.

A Region That Swung — and Is Swinging Back

The Valley, home to about 1.5 million people, was once reliably Democratic. In 2024, Trump won Hidalgo County, home to McAllen, with 51 percent of the vote — a three-point margin four years after Joe Biden had carried it by 17 points. In neighbouring Cameron County, Trump won by about five points after losing it by 13 in 2020. Discontent over the border — crossings that rose after the COVID-era asylum policy ended, and a region left to deal with the fallout — was credited in part with that swing.

Two years on, the enforcement has moved inland, and the mood with it. Jose Arizpe, a 40-year-old Brownsville resident and regular Republican voter, still calls the change positive, pointing to fewer asylum seekers waiting in the US for their cases. But Martin Torres, 55, who cast an early ballot for Democrats at a Brownsville library, said he first supported Trump on border policy before domestic enforcement — and its impact on the local workforce — soured his view. A Caminos Institute report estimated the region has lost $180.6 million in economic activity due to the administration's immigration policies, including in construction and restaurants.

Others point to discrimination. The US Supreme Court has ruled that border agents can physically block asylum seekers from reaching US soil, and last year lifted a lower-court order barring officials from considering apparent race or ethnicity and language on patrol — which rights groups say effectively allows racial profiling. A Texas state law also lets local officials stop people they suspect entered the country illegally. George Castorena, a 46-year-old education worker voting for change, said he sees a lot of discrimination going on.

What the Polling Says

The ACLU of Texas poll, conducted by Change Research among 1,031 adults in El Paso County and the four Rio Grande Valley counties between August 25 and September 2, found 53 percent of border residents think state and local immigration enforcement makes life harder without making their communities safer, against only 34 percent who say it makes them safer. Sixty-three percent believe ICE tactics have gone too far, and 64 percent want local and state law enforcement to prioritise preventing and solving crime over immigration enforcement.

The numbers align with polling showing Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido leading Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz, and Democratic incumbent Vicente Gonzalez leading Republican challenger Eric Flores, in two Valley congressional districts Republicans had viewed as strong prospects. "People along the border in the Rio Grande Valley are not in alignment with what they probably voted for back in 2024," said Osvaldo Grimaldo, a policy strategist at the ACLU of Texas.

"God forgives, but the government doesn't."

— Eli Lara, lead pastor, New Life Family Church, McAllen, on a congregant deported over a past drug conviction

What November 3 Can and Cannot Change

Midterms offer only incremental change on an issue this entrenched. A Democratic House would at best block further enforcement funding and open investigations. Senate control could turn on the Texas contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico. Even an upset win by Democrat Gina Hinojosa for governor — which would end Governor Greg Abbott's use of state agencies to support federal enforcement — would be constrained by a likely Republican state legislature.

For Garcia, who volunteers with the Hidalgo County Young Democrats, the galvanising cases are local: the assault of a 17-year-old by immigration agents in Alamo, and the fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston in July 2026. People told her politics does not affect them, she said — until the raids made them realise it does.

nri_angle: The Valley's story is the national one for immigrant communities, including Indian families in Texas: enforcement has shifted from the border to workplaces, hearings and missed court dates inside the country, and the November 3 result will shape funding and oversight of that machinery.
